The '''Bakhshali manuscript''' is an ancient Indian mathematical text written on [[Birch bark document|birch bark]] that was found in 1881 in the village of [[Bakhshali]], [[Mardan]] (near [[Peshawar]] in present-day [[Pakistan]], historical [[Gandhara]]). It is perhaps "the oldest extant manuscript in [[Indian mathematics]]".<ref name=HayashiEncy/> In 2017, Oxford University carbon-dated samples taken from three folios to 224–383 CE and 885–993 CE. In October 2024, Oxford University revised their earlier dating to 799–1102 CE.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Radiocarbon dating of the Bakhshālī manuscript |url=https://www.arch.ox.ac.uk/publication/2038638/ora-hyrax |access-date=2024-12-30 |website=www.arch.ox.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> The manner and timing of the publication of the 2017 test dates was criticised by a group of Indian mathematical historians (Plofker et al. 2017<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Houben |first=Jan E. M. |date=2018-01-01 |title=Linguistic Paradox and Diglossia: the emergence of Sanskrit and Sanskritic language in Ancient India |url=https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/opli-2018-0001/html |journal=Open Linguistics |language=en |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=1–18 |doi=10.1515/opli-2018-0001 |issn=2300-9969}}</ref> and Houben 2018 §3<ref name="doi.org">Jan E.M. Houben "Linguistic Paradox and Diglossia: on the emergence of Sanskrit and Sanskritic language in Ancient India." De Gruyter Open Linguistics (Topical Issue on Historical Sociolinguistic Philology, ed. by Chiara Barbati and Christian Gastgeber.) OPLI – Vol. 4, issue 1: 1–18.  DOI: https://doi.org/10.1515/opli-2018-0001</ref>). Up until September 2024 the manuscript was regarded as the earliest known Indian use of a [[zero]] symbol.<ref name="Devlin">{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/sep/14/much-ado-about-nothing-ancient-indian-text-contains-earliest-zero-symbol|title=Much ado about nothing: ancient Indian text contains earliest zero symbol|last=Devlin|first=Hannah |date=13 September 2017|work=The Guardian|access-date=2017-09-14|issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref name="Bodleian Library">{{cite news |date=14 September 2017 |title=Carbon dating finds Bakhshali manuscript contains oldest recorded origins of the symbol 'zero' |work=Bodleian Libraries |url=https://www.glam.ox.ac.uk/article/carbon-dating-finds-bakhshali-manuscript-contains-oldest-recorded-origins-symbol-zero |access-date=2023-01-13}}</ref> It is written in a form of literary [[Sanskrit]] influenced by contemporary dialects.

==Discovery==
The manuscript was unearthed in a field in 1881.<ref name=NineChapters/> It was unearthed by a peasant in the village of [[Bakhshali]], which is near [[Mardan]], in present-day [[Khyber Pakhtunkhwa]], Pakistan.<ref name=HayashiEncy/> The first research on the manuscript was done by [[A. F. R. Hoernlé]].<ref name=HayashiEncy/>{{sfn|Hoernle|1887}} After his death, it was examined by G.R.Kaye, who edited the work and published it as a book in 1927.<ref name="Kaye review"/>

The extant manuscript is incomplete. It consists of 70 leaves of [[birch bark]],<ref name=HayashiEncy/><ref name=NineChapters/> whose intended order is not known.<ref name=HayashiEncy/> It is kept at the [[Bodleian Library]] at the University of Oxford<ref name=HayashiEncy/><ref name=NineChapters/> (MS. Sansk. d. 14), though folio are periodically loaned to museums.<ref>{{Cite web|title=London museum showcases India's contribution to science|url=https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/opinion/columns/vidya-ram/london-museum-showcases-indias-contribution-to-science/article9885555.ece|access-date=2022-02-03|website=www.thehindubusinessline.com|language=en}}</ref>

==Contents==
[[File:Bakhshali numerals 2.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.6|The numerals used in the Bakhshali manuscript, dated to sometime between the 3rd and 7th century AD.]]
The manuscript is a compendium of rules and illustrative examples. Each example is stated as a problem, the solution is described, and it is verified that the problem has been solved. The sample problems are in verse and the commentary is in prose associated with calculations. The problems involve [[arithmetic]], [[algebra]] and [[geometry]], including [[mensuration (mathematics)|mensuration]]. The topics covered include fractions, square roots, [[arithmetic progression|arithmetic]] and [[geometric progression]]s, solutions of simple equations, [[simultaneous linear equations]], [[quadratic equations]] and [[indeterminate equations]] of the second degree.<ref name="Kaye review"/><ref name=Plofker>{{citation |last=Plofker |first=Kim |author-link=Kim Plofker |title=Mathematics in India|title-link= Mathematics in India (book) |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-691-12067-6 |page=158}}</ref>

===Composition===
The manuscript is written in an earlier form of [[Sharada script]], a script which is known for having been in use mainly from the 8th to the 12th century in the northwestern part of the [[Indian subcontinent]], such as [[Kashmir]] and neighbouring regions.<ref name=HayashiEncy/> The language of the manuscript,{{efn|Variously described either as an "irregular Sanskrit" {{harv|Kaye|2004|p=11}}, or as the so-called Gāthā dialect, the literary form of the Northwestern Prakrit, which combined elements of Sanskrit and [[Prakrit]] and whose use as a literary language predated the adoption of Classical Sanskrit for this purposely.{{harv|Hoernle|1887|p=10}} }} though intended to be [[Sanskrit]], was significantly influenced in its phonetics and morphology by a local artist dialect or dialects, and some of the resultant linguistic peculiarities of the text are shared with [[Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit]]. The overlying dialects, though sharing affinities with [[Apabhraṃśa]] and with Old [[Kashmiri language|Kashmiri]], have not been identified precisely.{{sfn|Hayashi|1995|p=54}} It is probable that most of the rules and examples had been originally composed in Sanskrit, while one of the sections was written entirely in a dialect.<ref>Section VII 11, corresponding to folio 46{{sup|''v''}}.{{harv|Hayashi|1995|p=54}}</ref> It is possible that the manuscript might be a compilation of fragments from different works composed in a number of language varieties.{{sfn|Hayashi|1995|p=54}} Hayashi admits that some of the irregularities are due to errors by scribes or may be orthographical.{{sfn|Hayashi|1995|p=26}}

A [[Colophon (publishing)|colophon]] to one of the sections states that it was written by a [[brahmin]] identified as "the son of ''Chajaka''", a "king of calculators," for the use of ''Vasiṣṭha''{{'}}s son ''Hasika''. The brahmin might have been the author of the commentary as well as the scribe of the manuscript.<ref name=Plofker/> Near the colophon appears a broken word ''rtikāvati'', which has been interpreted as the place ''Mārtikāvata'' mentioned by [[Varāhamihira]] as being in northwestern India (along with ''[[Takshasila|Takṣaśilā]]'', ''[[Gandhara|Gandhāra]]'' etc.), the supposed place where the manuscript might have been written.<ref name=HayashiEncy/>

===Mathematics===
The manuscript is a compilation of mathematical rules and examples (in verse), and prose commentaries on these verses.<ref name=HayashiEncy/> Typically, a rule is given, with one or more examples, where each example is followed by a "statement" (''nyāsa'' / ''sthāpanā'') of the example's numerical information in tabular form, then a computation that works out the example by following the rule step-by-step while quoting it, and finally a verification to confirm that the solution satisfies the problem.<ref name=HayashiEncy/> This is a style similar to that of [[Bhāskara I]]'s commentary on the ''gaṇita'' (mathematics) chapter of the [[Āryabhaṭīya]], including the emphasis on verification that became obsolete in later works.<ref name=HayashiEncy/>

The rules are [[algorithm]]s and techniques for a variety of problems, such as systems of linear equations, quadratic equations, arithmetic progressions and arithmetico-geometric series, computing [[square root]]s approximately, dealing with [[negative number]]s (profit and loss), measurement such as of the fineness of gold, etc.<ref name=NineChapters/>

<u>Equality of Two Uniformly Accelerated Growths</u>

Let,
<math>
S_1 = a + (a + d) + (a + 2d) + \ldots \text{ to } n \text{ terms,}
</math>  
<math>
S_2 = b + (b + e) + (b + 2e) + \ldots \text{ to } n \text{ terms,}
</math>

If these two are equal, we must have<br />
<math>
(n - 1)d + 2a = (n - 1)e + 2b
</math><br />
<math>
n = 2(b - a) / (d - e) + 1
</math><br />

This formula is contained in ''Bakshali Manuscript'', folio 4v, rule 17 (Kaye III, p. 176) as follows:
<blockquote>
''{{IAST|Ādyor viśeṣa dviguṇam cayasaṃdhiḥ-vibhājitam}}''<br/>
''{{IAST|Rūpādhikaṃ tathā kālaṃ gati sāmyam tadā bhavet.}}''
</blockquote>

"Twice the difference of the initial terms divided by the difference of the common differences is increased by one. That will be time (represented by <math>n</math>, cf. kāla iha padasyopalakṣaṇam) when the distances moved (by the two travellers) will be same."

<blockquote>
''{{IAST|Dvayāditricayaś caiva dvicayatryādikottaraḥ}}''<br/>
''{{IAST|Dvayo ca bhavate paṃthā kena kālena sāsyatāṃ kriyate?}}''
</blockquote>

The accompanying example reads:
"The initial speed (of a traveller) is 2 and subsequent daily increment is 3. That of another, these are 3 initially and 2 as increment. Find in what time will their distances covered attain equality."

The working is lost, but the answer, by the formula in the previous example,
<math>
n = 2(3 - 2) / (3 - 2) + 1 = 3 \text{ days.}
</math>

<ref>
{{cite journal
 |last= Gupta
 |first= R. C.
 |title= Some Equalization Problems from the Bakhshali Manuscript
 |journal= Indian Journal of History of Science
 |volume= 21
 |issue= 1
 |year= 1986
 |publisher= Department of Mathematics, Birla Institute of Technology
 |location= Ranchi, India
 |page= 58
}}
</ref>

===Numerals and zero===
[[File:Bakhshali manuscript zero detail.jpg|thumb|Bakhshali manuscript, detail of the numeral "zero".]]
The Bakhshali manuscript uses numerals with a place-value system, using a dot as a place holder for zero.<ref name="MacTutor Zero">
{{cite web
| title =        A history of zero
| author1 = J. J. O'Connor 
| author2 =       E. F. Robertson
| publisher =    [[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive]]
| url =         https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Zero/ 
|date=November 2000
| access-date =   24 July 2022
}}
</ref><ref name="Bodleian Library"/>
The dot symbol came to be called the ''shunya-bindu'' (literally, the dot of the empty place). References to the concept are found in Subandhu's ''[[Vasavadatta]]'', which has been dated between 385 and 465 by the scholar Maan Singh even though the dates are disputed by other scholars<ref name="singh1">Singh, Maan (1993). ''Subandhu'', New Delhi: Sahitya Akademi, {{ISBN|81-7201-509-7}}, pp.&nbsp;9–11.</ref>

Prior to the 2017 carbon dating, a 9th-century inscription of zero on the wall of a temple in [[Gwalior]], Madhya Pradesh, was once thought to be the oldest Indian use of a zero symbol.<ref name="Bodleian Library"/>

==Date==
In 2017, samples from 3 folios of the corpus were [[radiocarbon dating|radiocarbon dated]] to three different centuries and empires: 224–383 CE for folio 16 ([[Indo-Scythians|Indo-Scythian]]),  680–779 CE for folio 17 ([[Turk Shahis]]), and 885–993 CE for folio 33 ([[Saffarid dynasty]]). If the dates are valid, it is unclear how folios from different centuries came to be collected and buried.<ref name="Devlin"/><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.arch.ox.ac.uk/reader/items/oxford-radiocarbon-accelerator-unit-dates-the-worlds-oldest-recorded-origin-of-the-zero-symbol.html|title=Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit dates the world's oldest recorded origin of the zero symbol|last=Mason|first=Robyn|date=14 September 2017|work=School of Archaeology, University of Oxford|access-date=2017-09-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170914215605/http://www.arch.ox.ac.uk/reader/items/oxford-radiocarbon-accelerator-unit-dates-the-worlds-oldest-recorded-origin-of-the-zero-symbol.html|archive-date=2017-09-14|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Bodleian Library"/>

However, on 14 October 2024, Oxford University, having revised its findings from a second run of carbon dating tests in 2018, dated the Bakshali manuscripts to 799 - 1102 CE, with folio 16 being redated to 931-1032 CE.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chivall |first=David |last2=Lladó-Buisán |first2=Virginia |last3=Howell |first3=David |last4=Evison |first4=Gillian |title=Radiocarbon dating of the Bakhshālī manuscript |url=https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:5a6d1dd7-f20c-4209-adb6-33849f5b08f4/files/snp193c210 |format=PDF |agency=Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit, University of Oxford}}</ref>
{| class="wikitable"
|+ Calibrated Radiocarbon date ranges, 95.4% confidence interval, AD<ref>{{Cite web |last=Howell |first=David |date=3 July 2017 |title=Carbon dating reveals Bakhshali manuscript is centuries older than scholars |url=https://ia903104.us.archive.org/18/items/BodleianBakshaliStatement2017/Bodleian%20Library_Bakhshali%20Research%20Statement_2017.pdf |website=Bodleian Libraries}}</ref><ref name="Ox2024">{{Cite web |last=Chivall |first=David |date=2024 |title=Radiocarbon dating of the Bakhshālī manuscript |url=https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:5a6d1dd7-f20c-4209-adb6-33849f5b08f4/files/snp193c210}}</ref>

The publication of the radio carbon dates, initially via non-academic media, led [[Kim Plofker]], Agathe Keller, [[Takao Hayashi]], [[Clemency Montelle]] and Dominik Wujastyk to publicly object to the library making the dates globally available, usurping academic precedence: 
{{Blockquote
|text=We express regret that the Bodleian Library kept their carbon-dating findings embargoed for many months, and then chose a newspaper press-release and YouTube as media for a first communication of these technical and historical matters. The Library thus bypassed standard academic channels that would have permitted serious collegial discussion and peer review prior to public announcements. While the excitement inspired by intriguing discoveries benefits our field and scholarly research in general, the confusion generated by broadcasting over-eager and carelessly inferred conclusions, with their inevitable aftermath of caveats and disputes, does not.|author=Plofker et al.|title=The Bakhshālī Manuscript: A Response to the Bodleian Library’s Radiocarbon Dating, 2017<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Plofker |first1=Kim |last2=Keller |first2=Agathe |last3=Hayashi |first3=Takao |last4=Montelle |first4=Clemency |last5=Wujastyk |first5=Dominik |date=2017-10-06 |title=The Bakhshālī Manuscript: A Response to the Bodleian Library's Radiocarbon Dating |url=https://journals.library.ualberta.ca/hssa/index.php/hssa/article/view/22 |journal=History of Science in South Asia |language=en |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=134–150 |doi=10.18732/H2XT07 |issn=2369-775X|doi-access=free }}</ref>}}

Referring to the detailed reconsideration of the evidence by Plofker et al., Sanskrit scholar, Jan Houben remarked: 
{{Blockquote
|text=If the finding that samples of the same manuscript would be centuries apart is not based on mistakes ... there are still some factors that have evidently been overlooked by the Bodleian research team: the well-known divergence in exposure to cosmic radiation at different altitudes and the possible variation in background radiation due to the presence of certain minerals in exposed, mountainous rock have nowhere been taken into account.<ref name="doi.org"/>}}

Prior to the proposed radiocarbon dates of the 2017 study, most scholars agreed that the physical manuscript was a copy of a more ancient text, whose date had to be estimated partly on the basis of its content. Hoernlé thought that the manuscript was from the 9th century, but the original was from the 3rd or 4th century.{{efn|G. R. Kaye, on the other hand, thought in 1927 that the work was composed in the 12th century,<ref name=HayashiEncy/><ref name="Kaye review">
{{cite journal
| title =        Book Review: G. R. Kaye, The Bakhshâlî Manuscript—A Study in Mediaeval Mathematics, 1927
| author =       Bibhutibhusan Datta
| journal =    Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.
| url =          https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183493367
| volume = 35 |number=4 |year=1929 |pages=579–580
| doi = 10.1090/S0002-9904-1929-04778-5
| doi-access =free
}}</ref> but this was discounted in recent scholarship. G. G. Joseph wrote, "It is particularly unfortunate that Kaye is still quoted as an authority on Indian mathematics."<ref>{{citation |last=Joseph |first=G. G. |year=2000 |title=The Crest of the Peacock, non-European roots of Mathematics |publisher=Princeton University Press|pages=215–216}}</ref>}} Indian scholars assigned it an earlier date. Datta assigned it to the "early centuries of the Christian era".<ref name="Kaye review"/> Channabasappa dated it to AD 200–400, on the grounds that it uses mathematical terminology different from that of [[Aryabhata]].<ref name=MacTutor>
{{cite web
| title =        The Bakhshali manuscript
| author1 = J. J. O'Connor 
| author2 =       E. F. Robertson
| publisher =    [[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive]]
| url =          http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Bakhshali_manuscript.html
|date=November 2000
| access-date =   24 July 2022
| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070809014215/http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/Bakhshali_manuscript.html| archive-date= 9 August 2007|url-status= live}}</ref> Hayashi noted some similarities between the manuscript and [[Bhaskara I]]'s work (AD 629), and said that it was "not much later than Bhaskara I".<ref name=HayashiEncy/>

To settle the date of the Bakhshali manuscript, language use and especially palaeography are other major parameters to be taken into account. In this context Houben observed: "it is difficult to derive a linear chronological difference from the observed linguistic variation," and therefore it is necessary to "take quite seriously the judgement of palaeographists such as Richard Salomon who observed that, what he teleologically called “Proto-Śāradā,” “first emerged around the middle of the seventh century” (Salomon 1998: 40). This excludes the earlier dates attributed to manuscript folios on which a fully developed form of Śāradā appears."<ref name="doi.org"/>
